sourcedFrom: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 (none printed)
cleanIntro: Traditions publishes one book for its musket reproductions, FIT-69, and it names no model — the cover scopes it by action type and nothing inside prints a model designation. Every step below is one that book states generally for a musket-cap percussion musket. This is NOT the sidelock book: it prescribes musket caps rather than #10/#11 percussion caps, it accounts for barrel bands on a full stock, and it forbids removing the bolster, drum or breech from the barrel.

steps.title: Treat it as loaded before anything else
steps.action: Point the muzzle somewhere safe and work on the assumption that the musket is charged and capped until the ramrod says otherwise. There is no action to open and no chamber to look into on a muzzleloader.
steps.quote: WARNING: ALWAYS POINT THE MUZZLE IN A SAFE DIRECTION AND TREAT THE FIREARM AS IF IT WAS LOADED AND CAN FIRE. WARNING: CONFIRM THE FIREARM IS UNCHARGED AND UNPRIMED BEFORE CONDUCTING ANY OF THE FUNCTION TESTS.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 5. Function Test For Sidelock Muzzleloaders, printed p.18

steps.title: Half-cock and lift the musket cap off the nipple
steps.action: Thumb the hammer back to half cock so it clears the cone, then take the musket cap off. Keep the muzzle downrange while you do it — a capped nipple is a live ignition train and the hammer is sitting on top of it.
steps.quote: Percussion Models: With the gun pointed in a safe direction, upward and down range, move the hammer to the half-cock position and remove the musket cap from the nipple.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 11. Depriming Your Muzzleloader After Firing, printed p.29

steps.title: Musket caps, not #10 or #11 percussion caps
steps.action: This is the tell that separates a musket reproduction from a sporting sidelock: the cone is noticeably larger and takes a four-wing musket cap. Traditions asks you to check your own nipple rather than assume, and warns off the small percussion caps entirely.
steps.quote: Note: Please take note of your nipple size on Percussion models and use correctly-sized musket caps. If you have a large nipple on your sidelock muzzleloader, it is most likely that this rifle uses musket caps. Therefore, you should not use #10 or #11 percussion caps.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 7. Basic Equipment For Shooting A Sidelock, printed p.22
steps.warn: Therefore, you should not use #10 or #11 percussion caps.

steps.title: Mark the ramrod where it leaves the muzzle
steps.action: Send the ramrod down the bore and mark it level with the muzzle, with the same tip fitted every time. On a long musket barrel this is the only measurement you get.
steps.quote: 1. Insert the ramrod down the bore of the barrel and mark it at the point where it exits the muzzle. In the event that the ramrod completely enters the barrel, take note of the distance between the end of the ramrod and the muzzle.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 5. Function Test For Sidelock Muzzleloaders, printed p.18

steps.title: Read the mark against the breech end
steps.action: Lay the rod beside the barrel with the mark at the muzzle. The far end should reach the nipple; two inches short means powder, a ball, or both are still in there.
steps.quote: 2. Remove the ramrod and lay it alongside the barrel. 3. Align the reference mark on the ramrod even with the end of the muzzle. If the gun is unloaded, the other end of the ramrod should be even with the nipple of a percussion gun or touch hole area of a flintlock. If it is significantly higher (2'') than that, the barrel is probably either obstructed or loaded. In either case, this situation must be resolved before continuing with the loading and shooting procedures.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 5. Function Test For Sidelock Muzzleloaders, printed p.18

steps.title: A charged barrel is not cleared by firing it
steps.action: If the rod finds an obstruction, go to the uncharging procedure — barrel out of the stock, breech end soaked in hot water for half an hour, ball puller on the rod. Traditions expressly tells you not to shoot it out.
steps.quote: 4. If you find an obstruction, please consult the "Unloading & Uncharging Your Rifle" section of this manual. Do not attempt to clear the barrel by firing.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 5. Function Test For Sidelock Muzzleloaders, printed p.18

steps.title: This strip is owed after every session, not occasionally
steps.action: Black powder residue is corrosive and pulls moisture out of the air overnight. Traditions makes the field disassembly a requirement after every firing session, not a periodic service.
steps.quote: The field disassembly procedure is most often used for general cleaning, lubricating and inspecting your rifle. It must be completed after each shooting session. This procedure allows for quickly cleaning, lubrication and inspection of all important parts and assemblies.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Field Cleaning & Disassembly Procedure, printed p.37

steps.title: Ramrod, pins, tang screw, bands, barrel, lock
steps.action: In that order. Drive the tenon pins or wedges out of the forend from one side, back the tang screw out of the rear of the barrel, then slide any barrel bands off TOWARD THE MUZZLE — a full-stock musket is banded, and driving a band the other way splits the forend. The barrel then lifts out, and the lock plate screws come out last.
steps.quote: DISASSEMBLY PROCEDURE 1. Remove ramrod. 2. Carefully tap barrel tenon wedge(s) or tenon pins to drive them out the opposite side of the forend. Take care not to damage the stock. 3. Remove tang screw located at the very back end of the barrel. 4. If your muzzleloader has barrel bands, carefully remove them from the barrel/stock by taking them off in the direction of the muzzle. 5. Lift barrel from stock. Light tapping may be necessary to initially break the barrel free of the stock. 6. After completing these steps, you may now remove your lock plate screws and lock plate for cleaning.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Disassembly Procedure, printed p.39

steps.title: Stop here: the bolster, drum and breech stay in the barrel
steps.action: This is the one operation the maker forbids. The bolster or drum and the breech are torqued to interlock, and unscrewing either destroys that lockup. Access to the fire channel is through the nipple seat, and that is deliberate.
steps.quote: Important: Never remove the bolster/drum or breech from the barrel. They have been installed at the factory such that they interlock with each other for maximum lockup strength. The removal or alteration of these key parts will compromise the performance of your gun, void your warranty, and can create an unsafe situation.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — General Cleaning, printed p.38
steps.warn: The removal or alteration of these key parts will compromise the performance of your gun, void your warranty, and can create an unsafe situation.

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: Barrel, stock, lock, bands and ramrod — that is the whole strip this manual publishes, and it is the boundary Traditions sets. Everything after this is cleaning. Deep Clean covers the nipple threads, the oil purge, the reassembly order and the function test.
steps.quote: WARNING: NEVER DISASSEMBLE YOUR FIREARM beyond the instructions outlined in this manual. Improper disassembly or reassembly of your firearm may create a dangerous situation which can lead to serious injury or death to you or others or also the destruction of property.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 1. Your Safety Responsibilities, printed p.6

steps.title: Take the nipple out before you wet anything
steps.action: With the nipple out the barrel has a second opening, and that is what turns the bore into something you can flush rather than swab. It also gets the cone itself where you can scrub it.
steps.quote: 1. Remove the nipple of a percussion gun or the touch hole liner from a flintlock.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — General Cleaning, printed p.38

steps.title: Pump solvent down the muzzle and out the breech
steps.action: Patched jag on a rod, warm soapy water or black powder solvent down the bore until it comes out of the nipple seat. Black powder fouling is water-soluble, which is why hot water genuinely works here.
steps.quote: 2. Wrap a cleaning patch around a loading jag attached to a ramrod. 3. Pump warm soapy water or a black powder solvent down the muzzle and out the hole(s) in the breech end of the gun.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — General Cleaning, printed p.38

steps.title: Pipe-cleaner the fire channel, then rinse and dry
steps.action: Work a pipe cleaner through the fire channel in the bolster until it comes out clean. This passage carries the cap's flash into the charge; caked residue in it is the ordinary cause of a musket misfire.
steps.quote: 4. Insert a pipe cleaner into the bolster/drum fire channel to help remove any residue. 5. Rinse and dry barrel.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — General Cleaning, printed p.38

steps.title: Stand the barrel breech-down and draw solution through it
steps.action: Breech end into a pail of solution, then pump a patched jag up and down the bore. The barrel works as a syringe and pulls the solution up past the fouling — far more effective on a long barrel than pushing patches through.
steps.quote: 1. An easy procedure is to stand the barrel in a pail of cleaning solution, breech end down. 2. With a cleaning patch on a loading/cleaning jag attached to the end of a ramrod, draw the solution in and out of the barrel by means of a pumping action to create suction.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Cleaning Process, printed p.40

steps.title: Wipe the outside, rinse warm, dry it immediately
steps.action: Wipe down the barrel exterior and the rest of the gun with the same solution, then rinse with warm water and dry at once. Warm steel dries itself; a barrel left standing wet is a pitted barrel.
steps.quote: 3. Wipe the exterior surfaces of the barrel and the rest of the gun with a cloth dipped in the same cleaning solution. 4. Rinse the barrel with warm water and immediately dry the barrel
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Cleaning Process, printed p.40

steps.title: Oil every metal surface, the inside of the lock plate included
steps.action: The lock plate and trigger assembly can come out of the stock for this. Once everything is dry, oil all the metal — the inside of the lock plate is named explicitly because it sits closest to the flash and is the surface most often skipped.
steps.quote: 5. The lock plate and trigger assembly can be removed from the stock, as well as the other metal components. 6. When the gun parts are dry, treat all metal surfaces, including the inside of the lock plate, with a light coating of a rust preventative or gun oil. Reassemble.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Cleaning Process, printed p.40

steps.title: Lube the nipple threads before it goes back in
steps.action: WonderLube on the nipple threads every time. Dry threads in a fouled barrel seize, and a seized musket nipple usually ends up drilled out.
steps.quote: CAUTION: Each time the gun is cleaned, be sure to remove the nipple. (On flint-lock models remove the touch hole.) Clean the fire channel in the bolster with a pipe cleaner or the like. Reinstall the nipple (or touch hole). Be sure to always lube the threads of the nipple or touch hole liner with WonderLube to insure their easy future removal.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Cleaning Process, printed p.40

steps.title: Store it cool, dry and out of a case
steps.action: A gun case holds moisture against the steel, which is the opposite of what a black powder gun needs after cleaning. Cool, dry and locked.
steps.quote: 7. Store the gun in a cool, dry place which can be securely locked. Storage in a gun case is not recommended. It may retain moisture and hasten corrosion.
steps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Cleaning Process, printed p.40

deepSteps.title: Inspect the nipple threads and its seat in the barrel
deepSteps.action: Look at both halves of the thread, not just the nipple. Traditions warns that leaning on the wrench cross-threads the recess in the barrel — damage that is permanent and that also stops the nipple sealing gas at the cone.
deepSteps.caution: During installation and removeal, excess pressure on the nupple can cause cross-threading and this can permanently damage the barrel.
deepSteps.quote: NOTE: Be sure to inspect the threads on both the nipple and nipple recess hole in the barrel. During installation and removeal, excess pressure on the nupple can cause cross-threading and this can permanently damage the barrel. It can also prohibit a solid gas seal in the communcation area.
deepSteps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Field Cleaning & Disassembly Procedure, printed p.37

deepSteps.title: Coat the ignition threads on a schedule
deepSteps.action: The maker asks for this before first firing and regularly thereafter, and whenever a new nipple goes in. It is the difference between a part that comes out with a wrench and one that has to be destroyed to remove.
deepSteps.quote: Caution: Before loading and firing your new Traditions™ gun for the first time, remove the nipple and clean-out screw from the bolster or the touch hole liner from the flintlock and coat the threads of each with Traditions™ WonderLube. This will help in future removal.
deepSteps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Field Cleaning & Disassembly Procedure, printed p.37

deepSteps.title: Purge the oil out of the bore and ignition channel
deepSteps.action: Preservative oil in the breech is what kills a first shot. Traditions has you run a clean white patch fully down the bore, fire a musket cap through it, and read the patch — repeat until it comes out dry.
deepSteps.quote: Method 2. Make sure the rifle is unloaded and pointed in a safe direction. Place a clean cleaning patch on the cleaning jag end of a ramrod. Insert the ramrod with clean white patch attached. Point the gun, with ramrod fully inserted, in a safe direction and fire a musket cap. Remove ramrod. Observe amount of residue on the patch. Reinsert the ramrod with clean patch. Repeat this procedure until the patch comes out relatively free of oil and moisture.
deepSteps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 6. Initial Cleaning, printed p.21

deepSteps.title: Reassemble in the maker's order
deepSteps.action: Barrel into the stock channel first, then the tang screw, then the tenon wedges or pins, ramrod last. Starting the tang screw before the pins go in is what lets the barrel settle into its own bedding instead of being pinned crooked.
deepSteps.quote: REASSEMBLY PROCEDURE 1. Gently reinstall the barrel back into the stock channel. 2. Reinstall the tang screw with a screwdriver. 3. Gently tap the barrel tenon wedge(s) or tenon pins back into the barrel and stock. 4. Reinstall the ramrod.
deepSteps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Reassembly Procedure, printed p.40

deepSteps.title: Check the ramrod retention spring before the rod goes back
deepSteps.action: If the lock came out, the ramrod retention spring rides on the front lock screw. Confirm it is back on that screw before you push the ramrod home — get this wrong and the rod will not stay in the thimbles, or the spring ends up loose inside the stock.
deepSteps.quote: NOTE: If you removed your lock during this process, be sure to check that your ramrod retention spring is properly installed back onto your front lock screw prior to installing your ramrod back into the stock.
deepSteps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Reassembly Procedure, printed p.40

deepSteps.title: Function test before you call the musket done
deepSteps.action: Traditions puts this as a caution on the disassembly procedure itself: the rifle is not reassembled until the lock has been proved.
deepSteps.quote: Caution: Perform a function test as described earlier in this manual to confirm your rifle is fully operational and reassembly was correctly completed.
deepSteps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 15. Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly — Detailed Cleaning & Disassembly/Reassembly Procedure, printed p.39

deepSteps.title: Run the hammer and trigger test
deepSteps.action: Half cock and try the trigger — nothing moves. Then take it to full cock. The half-cock notch is the only safety this lock has, so a trigger that trips at half cock is a musket that goes back to a gunsmith, not to the range.
deepSteps.quote: 1. Cock the rifle by rotating the hammer rearward until you hear a metallic click and the hammer is locked into place. This means the rifle is now half-cocked and the safety feature is engaged. 2. Pull the trigger to ensure that the half-cock setting has arrested the pivoting ability of the trigger, as well as the hammer's ability to rotate forward. 3. Rotate the hammer to the fully cocked position.
deepSteps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 5. Function Test For Sidelock Muzzleloaders — Function testing the Hammer & Trigger, printed p.19

deepSteps.title: Leave the lock adjustment alone unless it misbehaves
deepSteps.action: The sear engagement screw on the tumbler is set at the factory. Turning it clockwise reduces engagement, and too little engagement is a hair trigger that can fire off a jar. If the lock passed the test above, do not touch it.
deepSteps.quote: If the lock of your gun functions properly as described in the Loading and Shooting Instructions, do not attempt to adjust it.
deepSteps.cite: Safety & Instruction Manual For Musket Reproduction Muzzleloaders — FIT-69 — 4. Learning The Basics Of The Traditions™ Musket Muzzeloader — Lock Adjustment, printed p.17

cleaning.name: Bore
tasks: Pump warm soapy water or black powder solvent from the muzzle out through the nipple seat
Stand the barrel breech-down in solution and draw it through with a patched jag
Rinse with warm water and dry the barrel immediately
Dry-patch the full length until the patches come out clean
Leave a light film of rust preventative or gun oil in the bore

cleaning.name: Ignition system
tasks: Remove the nipple every time the musket is cleaned
Pipe-cleaner the fire channel in the bolster until it runs clean
Inspect the threads on both the nipple and its recess in the barrel
Lube the nipple threads with WonderLube before reinstalling
Use correctly sized musket caps — not #10 or #11 percussion caps

cleaning.name: Lock, bands and metalwork
tasks: Wipe every exterior surface with a cloth dipped in the cleaning solution
Oil all metal surfaces including the inside of the lock plate
Clean under the barrel bands and refit them toward the muzzle
Check the ramrod retention spring is back on the front lock screw

cleaning.name: Storage
tasks: Store cool, dry, locked and out of a gun case
During long storage, check the bore and outside surfaces for pitting and rust

reassembly: If the lock came out, set the lock plate back into its mortise and start both lock plate screws by hand; the ramrod retention spring must be back on the front lock screw before either is tightened.
Reinstall the nipple with its threads lubed, finger-start it, and stop as soon as it seats — the threads in the barrel are the half you cannot replace.
Gently reinstall the barrel back into the stock channel.
Reinstall the tang screw with a screwdriver.
Gently tap the barrel tenon wedges or tenon pins back into the barrel and stock.
Slide any barrel bands back on and seat them in their positions.
Reinstall the ramrod, and confirm it is retained by the spring.
Traditions asks for a function test at this point to confirm the musket is fully operational and that reassembly was correctly completed.
fncheck: Half cock and pull the trigger — neither the trigger nor the hammer should move; that notch is the only safety this lock has. Full cock and push forward on the hammer to confirm it stays locked. Then, empty and pointed somewhere safe, let the hammer down under control and confirm it lands square on the nipple.
